abstract.p: Chronic heart failure (CHF) affects 1–2% of adults in developed countries, with up to 50% experiencing sleep-disordered breathing (SDB). Sacubitril/valsartan (sac/val) has shown potential benefits on respiratory function, but its effect on SDB remains uncertain. This study aims to evaluates the effectiveness of sac/val on SDB and respiratory function in CHF patients. Electronic searches were conducted based on MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science using MeSH terms and relevant keywords. Apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) and central apnea index (CAI) were used as primary outcome. Statistical analysis was performed using Stata 15.1 SE, with Cochrane Q and I² statistics used for heterogeneity assessment. Publication bias and sensitivity analyses were conducted using various methods. Risk of bias was assessed using the MINORS and ROB 2.0 tools. Seven studies met inclusion criteria. Results indicated that sac/val significantly reduced AHI (mean difference [MD], -3.56; P < 0.001) and increased mean oxygen saturation (MD = 0.61; P < 0.001), although there was a modest rise in CAI (MD = 0.30; P = 0.049). The pooled analysis indicated a 22% reduction in CSA patients. The analysis demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in AHI and an improvement in SpO2 during sleep after using sac/val. While these findings suggest improvements in SDB, further high-quality research is needed to confirm these results and explore underlying mechanisms.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) is a common complication in patients with chronic heart failure (CHF) and has been linked to a worse prognosis. Studies show that approximately 50% of patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) are affected by SDB1. SDB can be categorized into two subtypes: obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and central sleep apnea (CSA). Currently, OSA is recognized as an independent risk factor for developing CHF2, significantly increasing morbidity and mortality rates in affected patients3. In contrast, CSA is typically considered as an indicator of cardiac dysfunction and is often used clinically to assess CHF severity4,5. Both OSA and CSA can exacerbate CHF by disrupting the neurohumoral system and elevating sympathetic and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activity. The current clinical consensus is that the primary approach for managing SDB in patients with CHF is to optimize CHF management6,7. This includes enhancing medical therapy and implementing various non-pharmacologic interventions8. However, recent findings from the SERVE-HF trial and the ADVENT-HF study have raised concerns, as they demonstrated that adaptive servo-ventilation (ASV) devices are ineffective for treating CSA and may increase the risk of cardiovascular death9. This has intensified the search for effective treatment strategies for SDB in CHF patients.

Sacubitril–valsartan (Entresto™; LCZ696, sac/val) is a novel oral complex that combines the neprilysin inhibitor prodrug sacubitril with the angiotensin II type 1 receptor blocker valsartan. Approved in 2015 as a first-line treatment for patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) in New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classes II to IV, this drug has demonstrated a reduction in all-cause mortality among heart failure patients10,11. Specifically, sac/val, an alternative to the ACE inhibitor enalapril, lowers the incidence of cardiovascular death or hospitalization due to worsening congestive heart failure (CHF) by 20%12. Its therapeutic effects stem from its dual action on the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and the natriuretic peptide system (NP), which together decrease extracellular fluid retention, reduce sympathetic nervous system activity, and optimize hemodynamic parameters11.

Numerous investigations have been conducted to assess the efficacy and safety of sac/val in the management of HF patients. Most of these studies have utilized observational designs, with only a limited number being randomized controlled trials13–16. The mechanism by which sac/val improves SDB remains inconclusive. Some studies suggest that sac/val may increase cardiac output or reduce pleural fluid accumulation14. It may also enhance SDB by improving alveolar-capillary membrane function and reducing pulmonary congestion16. Identifying patients with SDB is also a key focus of ongoing research. Polysomnography (PSG) is an essential diagnostic tool for identifying sleep apnea syndrome, as it evaluates variables such as electroencephalogram, electrocardiogram, apnea frequency, and oxygen saturation levels to determine the presence and severity of sleep disorders17–19.

Despite the growing evidence of the significant benefits of this pharmacological intervention for managing HF and improving SDB, some studies suggest that the positive effects of evidence-based drug therapy on SDB in patients with HFrEF may be minimal11. In light of the absence of a published systematic review in this domain, it is imperative to synthesize the disparate research evidence in a scientific manner. Therefore, this initial systematic review and meta-analysis seeks to aggregate clinical evidence regarding the impact of sac/val on sleep quality in patients with SDB and HF.

The systematic review was reported adhering to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines20. The Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions served as a foundational resource, providing established protocols for the execution and documentation of meta-analytic studies. The methodology employed a structured, stepwise approach as delineated in the handbook, facilitating a thorough and systematic examination of the available evidence.

sec.title: Search strategy
sec.p: A comprehensive literature search was conducted across MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, and the Web of Science database, encompassing records from their inception up to November 2023, to identify pertinent studies. The search terms and keywords include ‘sacubitril valsartan sodium hydrate’, ‘hemipentahydrate’, ‘LCZ 696’, ‘sleep quality’, ‘sleep’, and ‘heart failure’, alongside pertinent keywords to refine the search criteria. Manual reference lists of the retrieved articles were screened to ensure comprehensive inclusion of potential studies. The specific search strategy for the targeted English-language databases is detailed in Supplementary Table 1.

sec.title: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
sec.p: The current investigation employed the Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes, and Study design (PICOS) framework to delineate the inclusion and exclusion criteria for the study. The inclusion criteria were as follows:

list-item.p: Population: Clinically diagnosed adult patients with CHF and SDB;
Intervention: Patients received sac/val treatment under any dosing regimen;
Comparator: For single-arm studies, a pre-post treatment comparison of sac/val; for double-arm studies, control group received enalapril treatment;

Outcomes: Study outcomes including apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), central apnea index (CAI), time spent with oxygen saturation below 90% (T90), mean SpO2 during sleep, or reduction ratio of central sleep apnea (CSA);
Study Design: Observational studies and randomized controlled trials (RCTs).

sec.p: The exclusion criteria were as follows:

list-item.p: Conference abstracts, case reports and review studies.
Studies with incomplete or missing data.
Studies not published in peer-reviewed journals.

sec.title: Data extraction
sec.p: Data extraction was conducted by two independent reviewers. In cases of discordance, a third reviewer mediated to reach a consensus. Data extraction from the selected studies included the following elements: authorship, year of publication, geographical location, participant sample size, study design, mean age, proportion of female participants, interventions for both experimental and control groups, and measured outcomes.

sec.title: Quality assessment
sec.p: To assess the methodological quality of the five observational studies, the Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies (MINORS) instrument was utilized21 The MINORS index for non-comparative studies consists of 8 items. Each item received a score of 0, 1, or 2, indicating high risk, unclear risk, and low risk of bias, respectively. Low risk of bias was defined as a MINORS score ≥ 12, moderate risk as a score ≥ 8 and < 12, and high risk as a score < 8.

For the two RCTs, the Cochrane Collaboration’s Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (ROB 2.0) was applied22. This tool evaluates five domains of potential bias: randomization process, deviations from the intended intervention, missing outcome data, measurement of outcomes, and selection of reported results. The domains and overall quality of the studies were categorized as high, low, or some concerns for bias.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The meta-analysis was conducted utilizing STATA SE 14.0 software, developed by StataCorp, located in College Station, Texas, USA. For continuous variables (AHI, CAI, T90, SpO2), the mean difference (MD) and its 95% confidence interval (CI) were used as effect indicators, while relative risk (RR) and its 95% CI were used for the incidence of CSA. Heterogeneity among the studies was assessed using the Cochrane Q test and the I-squared (I2) statistic. The hypothesis of random effects model was that the true effect size varies across studies. This model applies when the p-value ≤ 0.10 and the I² statistic ≥ 50%, indicating significant heterogeneity. Conversely, the fixed effects model assumes a common true effect size and is selected when heterogeneity is non-significant23. Subgroup analysis examined the impact of intervention duration and study design on outcomes. To detect publication bias, funnel plots, the Begg rank correlation test24., and Egger’s weighted regression were implemented25. If significant bias was found, a trim-and-fill analysis assessed its impact on study outcomes. Subgroup analyses investigated sources of heterogeneity as needed. Findings were further tested for robustness through sensitivity analysis using the leave-one-out method. Statistical significance was set at a p-value of less than 0.05.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: During the initial screening phase, 226 potentially relevant literature reports were identified. After excluding 86 duplicates, 71 reports were deemed ineligible based on title and abstract review. Following the assessment of 69 full-text manuscripts, 7 studies17,26–31 met the eligibility criteria for data extraction and meta-analysis. A flow diagram illustrating the study selection process is presented in Fig. 1.

caption.p: PRISMA flow chart for study screening and inclusion.

sec.p: This analysis included seven studies published between 2020 and 2023 that met the inclusion criteria. Participant cohorts ranged from 18 to 140 individuals from the United States, Germany, France, and Italy, mostly comprising elderly individuals (mean age = 65.27). The proportion of female participants varied from 16.67 to 23.53%. Refer to Table 1 for a demographic overview of participants. As for study design, the meta-analysis included two RCTs and five prospective single-arm studies. Two RCTs used enalapril as the control. The cardiac function of the enrolled patients was classified according to NYHA Class. Four studies included patients with NYHA Class II-IV heart failure, two studies included those with NYHA Class II-III, and one study included patients with NYHA Class I-III (Table 1).

sec.title: Quality assessment
sec.p: Quality assessment was performed among each included study by MINORS and ROB 2.0. The results of the included studies in this systematic review were at low risk (Table 1). The only concern was that the prospective studies included in the analysis were of limited size and did not furnish information pertinent to the prospective calculation of the sample size. Detailed quality assessment information was illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 2.

sec.title: AHI and CAI
sec.p: AHI diagnosed OSA in HF patients by counting apneas (complete airflow cessation for ≥ 10 s) and hypopneas (airflow reduction of ≥ 30% with a decline in blood oxygen of ≥ 3% or arousal) per hour during sleep. The CAI has often been employed to diagnose CSA by measuring central apneas (airflow cessation for ≥ 10 s without respiratory effort) per hour during sleep32. Both indices are crucial for the clinical diagnosis of SDB.

A meta-analysis of six studies17,27–31 was conducted to ascertain the impact of sacubitril/valsartan (sac/val) on AHI in patients with HF. The findings revealed a significant reduction in AHI following sac/val treatment (MD=−3.56; 95% CI: −5.52 to −1.59; P < 0.001; I² = 92.0%, P heterogeneity < 0.001), as depicted in Fig. 2A. Despite stratifying the analysis by intervention duration, the substantial heterogeneity observed in AHI could not be mitigated, as illustrated in Fig. 2B.

caption.p: Forest plot for AHI (A); Subgroups analysis of AHI by the intervention duration (B) and study design (C); Forest plot for CAI (D).

sec.p: The subgroup analysis explored the effects of interventions duration, either ≤ 3 months or > 3 months. There was no significant difference in both ≤ 3 months subgroup (MD=−3.93; 95% CI: −9.80 to 1.94; P = 0.19; I² = 87.4%, P heterogeneity = 0.005). However, there was a significant reduction of AHI in the > 3 months subgroup (MD=−3.52; 95% CI: −5.89 to −1.15; P = 0.004; I² = 94.4%, P heterogeneity < 0.001). The finding suggested that interventions duration could be a significant source of heterogeneity in the analysis. In the subgroup analysis of study design, both the non-RCT and RCT subgroups showed significant reductions in AHI, with the non-RCTs reporting a MD of −4.64 (95% CI: −5.62 to −3.66; P < 0.001; I² = 15.70%, P heterogeneity = 0.31) and the RCTs a MD of −1.17 (95% CI: −1.48 to −0.86; P < 0.001; I² = 0.00%, P heterogeneity = 0.95), indicating effective intervention across both study designs (Fig. 2C).

A meta-analysis of 2 studies29,31 was conducted to evaluate the impact of sac/val on CAI in patients with HF. The findings revealed an increase in CAI following sac/val treatment (MD = 0.30; 95% CI, 0.00 to 0.60; P = 0.049; I² = 39.1%, P heterogeneity = 0.200), as depicted in Fig. 2D. However, this result may be influenced by the over-weighting of a single study, making the outcome potentially unstable. Therefore, additional studies are needed to support this finding.

sec.title: T90 and SpO2
sec.p: The T90 parameter, which denotes the cumulative duration (minutes) of oxygen saturation levels below 90%, serves as a metric for assessing the severity of hypoxia associated with sleep apnea18,19.

In the evaluation of T90, data from four studies26,29–31 were incorporated. Although a reduction in T90 was observed post-treatment with sacubitril/valsartan (sac/val) in patients with HF, the change did not attain statistical significance (MD=−1.77; 95% CI, −7.92 to 4.39; P = 0.573; I²= 87.4%, P heterogeneity < 0.001), as detailed in Fig. 3A. The subgroup analysis for interventions duration included two groups: ≤3 months or > 3 months. There was no significant difference in the ≤ 3 months subgroup (MD=−13.10; 95% CI, −30.20 to 4.01; P = 0.13; I² = 88.7%, P heterogeneity < 0.001); while in the > 3 months subgroup, the change was statistical significance (MD = 3.00; 95% CI, 1.65 to 4.35; P < 0.001; P heterogeneity < 0.001) (Fig. 3B). The subgroup analysis for disease included two groups: LVEF ≤ 40% or HFrEF. In the subgroup analysis, the HFrEF group showed no significant difference in T90 (MD = 1.183; 95% CI, −1.838 to 4.20; P = 0.44; I² = 62.8%, P heterogeneity < 0.001) while in the LVEF ≤ 40% subgroup, the change was statistical significance (MD=−77.00; 95% CI, −113.278 to −40.722; P < 0.001; P heterogeneity < 0.001) (Fig. 3C). The mean SpO2 levels during sleep, reported in three studies17,28–30, demonstrated a significant increase following sac/val treatment (MD = 0.61; 95% CI, 0.43 to 0.79; I² = 49.4%, P heterogeneity = 0.139)17,28–30, as illustrated in Fig. 4A.

caption.p: Forest plot for T90 (A); Subgroups analysis of T90 by the intervention duration (B) and study design (C).
Forest plot for SpO2 (A); Forest plot for reduction ratio of CSA (B).

sec.title: Incidence of CSA
sec.p: Based on three included studies17,28,30, a significant reduction in CSA incidence was observed after sac/val treatment (95% CI: 0.11–0.34; I2 = 79.1%, P heterogeneity=0.008) (Fig. 4B).

sec.title: Publication bias and Sensitivity analysis
sec.p: The study employed funnel plots and statistical tests, specifically Begg’s and Egger’s tests, to assess potential publication bias. The funnel plots suggested possible publication bias in outcomes such as the AHI, CAI, T90, SpO2, and the reduction ratio of CSA (Supplementary Fig. 2). However, both Begg’s test and Egger’s test yielded P-values greater than 0.05, indicating no significant bias (Supplementary Table 3). No bias was detected in the analysis of CSA incidence (Supplementary Table 3). Sensitivity analyses using the leave-one-out method confirmed the robustness of all outcomes (Supplementary Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table 4).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis of seven studies evaluated the effect of sac/val on SDB in HF patients. Sac/val significantly reduced AHI and improved SpO₂ during sleep, with a modest but statistically significant reduction in CSA. Although the increase of CAI after sac/val treatment was observed and reached statistical significance, the absolute effect size was small and potentially unstable. Given the limited number of included studies and potential heterogeneity in patient characteristics and treatment protocols, this finding should be interpreted with caution. Further large-scale studies are needed to validate this observation.

Our results are consistent with previous observational studies reporting reduced AHI and improved SpO₂ after 3–6 months of sac/val treatment. However, differences in AHI improvement among studies warrant attention. Pelaia et al.17, Passino et al.30, and AWAKE-HF trial31 reached conflicting conclusions regarding the effectiveness of sac/val in improving nocturnal obstructive AHI in patients with obstructive sleep apnea syndrome. This suggests that baseline patient characteristics, the completeness of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) data17, and the duration of treatment may influence the efficacy of sac/val therapy.

Pelaia et al. proposed that sac/val improves AHI through combined effects of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), NT-proBNP, and tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), which together account for 43.3% of the variability in AHI17. Around these variables, various studies have explored underlying mechanisms. Sac/val may mitigate HF-related renal dysfunction by increasing natriuretic peptides and improving eGFR33–35. It may also enhance SpO₂ by reducing pulmonary edema and improving ventilation-perfusion matching36,37. Another key mechanism involves the circulatory and neuromodulatory functions of sac/val, which further enhance AHI and SpO2 by increasing cardiac output, shortening circulation time, inhibiting sympathetic nerve activity and chemoreflex sensitivity, reducing respiratory center disorders, and lowering the risk of upper airway obstruction38–40.

Based on similar mechanisms, the pooled analysis confirmed that sac/val reduces CSA incidence in HF patients. Studies conducted by Mapelli et al.28 and Pasino et al.30 also observed a reduction in sleep disturbances after treatment in patients presenting with CSA at baseline. Previous research has suggested that the improvement in sleep monitoring results following sac/val treatment is related to enhanced hemodynamics28. This conclusion was further validated by Apostolo et al.14, who demonstrated that hemodynamic improvements in patients with LVAD were associated with a reduction in apnea, particularly CSA. However, certain studies26,41,42 have posited that a decrease in CSA events post-sac/val treatment may signify a shift from CSA to OSA, a prevalent respiratory condition. Should a sufficient number of studies become available for future analysis, it would be feasible to compare and validate the incidence of OSA exacerbation events. Given that OSA predominantly manifests during nocturnal periods43–45, selecting appropriate diagnostic tools—such as CRM, portable monitors, or polysomnography—should balance accuracy with practicality in capturing real-world data.

In interpreting the findings, it is crucial to acknowledge certain limitations. Firstly, there may be a language bias, as the analysis was limited to articles published in English. Secondly, the limited number of studies, predominantly single-arm, restricts the ability to fully mitigate the impact of confounding factors on the study’s outcomes. Although funnel plots and statistical tests (Begg’s and Egger’s) did not indicate significant publication bias, the small number of studies may limit the sensitivity of these tests and increase the risk of undetected or underreported negative findings. Also, the included studies predominantly involved elderly male participants, which may limit the generalizability of our findings to younger individuals and female populations. Finally, the integration of before-and-after control studies and RCTs employing enalapril controls somewhat diminished the interpretability of the results. Nevertheless, given that this represents the inaugural quantitative review in this domain, a judicious expansion of the scope of included studies would facilitate a more comprehensive synthesis of the existing research.

In conclusion, this very first systematic review and meta-analysis found that sac/val effectively increases SpO2 levels and reduces AHI in patients with SDB and HF. These findings underscore a critical clinical implication that sac/val not only benefits cardiac function, but may also exert therapeutic effects on SDB by stabilizing respiratory control mechanisms and enhancing cardiopulmonary coupling. This treatment presents a promising option for managing SDB in clinical settings. To further validate the efficacy and safety of sac/val, future studies should involve larger sample sizes, a broader range of outcome indicators, and rigorous study designs. Large-scale, prospective trials should be conducted to evaluate clinical outcomes related to both CSA and OSA, including subgroup analyses based on age, sex, HF subtype, and baseline SDB characteristics.
